comments.author: deansaxe
comments.body:
Past CFP:

**Stop Counting Factors... Start Describing Authentication Events**
We began deploying multi-factor authentication because passwords provided insufficient security. More factors equals more
security, right? Yes, but we continue to see authentication attacks such as credential stuffing and phishing! The identity industry needs to stop thinking in the quantity of authentication factors, and start thinking about the properties of the authentication event. As we transition into the era of passkeys, it is time to consider how we describe the properties of our authentication event.

In this talk, we’ll demonstrate how identity providers and relying parties can communicate a consistent, composable collection
of authentication properties. To raise the security bar and provide accountability, these properties must communicate not only
about the authentication event, but about the security primitives underlying the event itself. These properties can be used to drive authentication and authorization decisions in standalone and federated environments, enabling clear, consistent application of security controls.

Dean Saxe, Principal Engineer, Office of the CTO, Beyond Identity
Pamela Dingle, Director of Identity Standards, Microsoft

comments.author: deansaxe
comments.body:
**Stop Counting Factors, Part Deux**

Two years ago, we stood on this stage and argued that the identity industry needed to stop counting authentication factors and start reasoning about the properties of the authentication event. The response from the community confirmed we had struck a nerve.

Since then, we have taken that argument from conference stage to standards body. We explored the idea further at IETF121 and OAuth Security Workshop 2025, and have since co-authored an IETF draft to formalize the terminology. We seek to develop a precise, interoperable vocabulary for describing what actually happened during authentication events.

In this talk, we will walk through the terminology the draft defines: what the terms mean, why the distinctions matter, and how identity providers and relying parties can use them today to drive clearer authentication and authorization decisions. 

We are not here to present a finished standard. We are here because standards development requires the identity community's input. If you have deployed passkeys, built policy engines on top of authentication context, or struggled to describe authentication events consistently across federated systems, your experience is directly relevant to this work.

Credential Security Properties: Progress Report

Two years ago, Pamela Dingle & Dean Saxe argued that the identity industry needed to stop counting authentication factors and start reasoning about the properties of the authentication event. issues.title: Add properties to describe zero-knowledge-proof credentials
issues.author: deansaxe
issues.body:
Raised in discussion by Nick Steele (OpenAI): the property set has no way to describe a zero-knowledge-proof credential.

## The gap

Zero-knowledge appears exactly once in the document, as a trailing example under Selective Disclosure:

> A mechanism by which some or all of the contents within a credential can be made available or unavailable under circumstances determined at presentation time. Example is an SD-JWT {{RFC9901}} or a ZKP.

SD-JWT and ZKP are offered as interchangeable examples of one property. They are not equivalent, and the difference is the one that matters most.

## Why this is a correctness problem, not a feature request

Appendix A states its own test: the tables exist "to validate that the property set is expressive enough to differentiate" credential types. Scored against the 14 types already in the appendix, a BBS+ credential and an SD-JWT VC come out **identical in every cell** of all 21 current properties — substantiation, dynamism, identifier binding, tamper proofness, audience restriction, validity window, selective disclosure, validity count, replayability, referential identity posture, and the whole containment, enrollment, compliance and recovery classes. A few of those cells are deployment-dependent rather than inherent, but none of them separate the two credential types.

By the appendix's own standard, the property set currently fails on ZKP credentials.

RFC 9901 Section 10.1 states the distinction authoritatively, so we can cite rather than assert it:

> Salted hash-based selective disclosure approaches, such as SD-JWT, cannot achieve complete issuer-verifier unlinkability because the issued credential with the Issuer's signature is directly presented to the Verifier, who can forward it to the Issuer.

RFC 9901 is already a declared reference in the draft. It also notes that batch issuance with distinct salts and key-binding keys buys verifier-to-verifier unlinkability but still does not solve issuer-verifier unlinkability.

## Proposed: one new property, possibly two

### 1. Unlinkability — Credential Presentation class

Alongside Replayability. Valued rather than boolean:

- **linkable** — presentations carry a static correlator (issuer signature, certificate serial, public key). SD-JWT VC, mdoc, X.509, bearer tokens.
- **verifier-unlinkable** — two presentations cannot be correlated by the verifier.
- **per-verifier pseudonymous** — unlinkable across verifiers, deliberately linkable within one. A real deployment mode, specified in `draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-per-verifier-linkability`.
- **issuer-unlinkable** — issuer and verifier colluding cannot map a presentation to an issuance.

W3C VC Data Model 2.0 Section 8 decomposes correlation into identifier-based (8.4), signature-based (8.5) and metadata-based (8.6), which may be a better basis for the value set than the four levels above. Worth deciding deliberately.

### 2. Predicate Proof — Credential Construction class

Alongside Selective Disclosure. The ability to prove a statement over an attribute without revealing the attribute: "over 21" rather than a date of birth.

Lower confidence on this one, and it should be decided separately. Plain BBS does **not** provide it — BBS gives selective disclosure plus unlinkable derived proofs. Predicates require a separate construction (range proofs such as Bulletproofs, or a SNARK circuit). So this property would read "no" for BBS and "yes" only for SNARK- or Bulletproof-based credentials. That is still a genuine differentiation, but it does not carry the SD-JWT contrast; unlinkability does that alone. If we want the minimum set, Unlinkability is the one that must land.

Recommendation: do **not** split Selective Disclosure itself. Leave it as field-level reveal and let these carry the distinction.

## Unlinkability is orthogonal to Referential Identity Posture

Expected objection: Pseudonymous and Anonymous posture values already cover this. They do not.

- A credential can be **Direct** posture and fully unlinkable — BBS proving a fact about the actual holder with no correlator.
- A credential can be **Pseudonymous** posture and perfectly linkable — the same pseudonym at every presentation is itself a correlator.

Posture is whose identity is asserted. Unlinkability is whether presentations can be correlated. Separate axes.

Note that Pseudonymous and Anonymous postures currently have no examples in the draft. ZKP credentials are the natural examples, so this issue also closes that gap.

## Out of scope, with reasons

- **Trusted setup** (BBS and STARKs transparent; Groth16 circuit-specific; PLONK universal). A property of the proof system, not of the credential's operation. Fails the inherence test and drags crypto-agility into a document that excludes it. It is discussed in the credential-systems literature, so expect it to be raised.
- **Issuer observability / phone-home at presentation.** Real security value, and the draft already gestures at it by distinguishing opaque-handle introspection. But mostly a deployment choice, so it fails inherence.
- **Blinded holder binding.** Better as a clarifying value on the existing Identifier Binding — binding exists, identifier is not revealed. W3C `vc-di-bbs` Section 4.1 names this "anonymous holder binding".

## Appendix rows

Add a **BBS+ anonymous credential** row so the new column visibly separates it from SD-JWT VC and mdoc.

Do **not** add a ZKP-over-mdoc row: ISO/IEC 18013-5 selective disclosure is hash-based via the Mobile Security Object, not zero-knowledge, and 18013-7 (2025) does not mandate ZKP. The composed-proof work is research, not standards.

Optional second row worth considering: a **Privacy Pass token** (RFC 9577 / RFC 9578, both published). Unlinkable but not an attribute credential, so it stress-tests the new property from a different direction.

## Citations available

- `draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures` — "The BBS Signature Scheme", rev 14, IRTF CFRG, not yet an RFC.
- `draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-blind-signatures` rev 05; `draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-per-verifier-linkability` rev 03. Neither published.
- RFC 9901 Section 10.1 — the SD-JWT unlinkability limitation. Already a declared reference.
- `VC-DATA-MODEL` — already points at VC 2.0 REC (2025-05-15). Section 8 is the privacy/correlation material.
- W3C `vc-di-bbs` (Data Integrity BBS Cryptosuites) — only a Working Draft, and dated April 2024. Cite with care, if at all.
- ETSI TR 119 476 v1.2.1 (July 2024) — compares hash-based and ZKP selective disclosure for eIDAS attestations. Useful informative anchor.

Terminology is fragmented: specs say "unlinkability", "unlinkable disclosure", "anonymous holder binding", "derived proofs"; the literature says "multi-show unlinkability", "issuer-verifier unlinkability", "issuer blindness". Whatever we pick should be defined in the draft and cited to where it is used. Note that W3C frames unlinkable disclosure as a *subtype* of selective disclosure ("presentations cannot be correlated between verifiers"), which sits in tension with treating it as a separate property — resolve that explicitly rather than by accident.

## Decisions needed

1. Unlinkability as one valued property, or split into verifier- and issuer-unlinkability?
2. Value set: the four levels above, or W3C's identifier/signature/metadata correlation decomposition?
3. Does Predicate Proof land in this round or get its own issue?
4. Is `vc-di-bbs` citable at Working Draft status, given it is 2.5 years stale?

pulls.title: Add appendix mapping credential types to security properties
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
## What changed

Adds a new back-matter appendix, **"Applying the Properties to Common Credential Types"**, to `draft-dingle-sec-credproperties.md`. It maps four credential types across all 27 properties, grouped into six tables (one per security class):

- **Password** (also covers API keys and client credentials)
- **Synced passkey**
- **Device-bound passkey** (hardware security token)
- **SPIFFE X.509-SVID** (mTLS certificate)

## Why

Provides worked examples to validate that the property set is expressive enough to differentiate real-world credential types.

## Reviewer notes

- Cells are pre-filled **only** where the document body already determines the value for that credential type — either by naming the type explicitly or using an unambiguous instance of it as an example (e.g. Containment=Uncontained for passwords, Dynamism=Dynamic for FIDO passkeys, Identifier Binding for the X.509-SVID). Every other cell is intentionally left blank for the authors to complete manually.
- No changes to normative text or existing sections; this is additive only.
- Deliberately conservative judgment calls (left blank rather than inferred) are worth a look: e.g. Validity Count for passwords (the doc's example is a *temporary* password), and Containment/Boundary Binding for the device-bound passkey (the doc's examples use a different credential type).

A credential becomes available for an operation only when a local user gesture is performed. This user gesture may also be called an activation factor (see 800-63-4). pulls.title: Add pre-commit hook to strip trailing whitespace
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
## What

Adds a tracked pre-commit hook that keeps trailing whitespace out of the draft sources, plus local-setup docs in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## Why

The "Update Editor's Copy" CI build runs `make lint`, whose `lint-whitespace` step **fails the entire build on any trailing whitespace**. This has broken the build repeatedly (#27, #33) even though the document itself compiles fine — the failures were purely trailing whitespace. This hook catches it locally before it reaches CI.

## How it works

- `.githooks/pre-commit` strips trailing whitespace from staged `*.md`, `*.xml`, and `*.org` files and re-stages them (matching the existing `.editorconfig` `trim_trailing_whitespace = true`).
- If a file has *unstaged* changes too, it is left untouched and the commit is blocked with instructions, to avoid staging unrelated edits.
- Zero external dependencies — POSIX `sh` + `perl` (already present on macOS and the CI image).

## Enabling (per clone)

Git does not auto-enable repo-tracked hooks, so each contributor runs once:

```sh
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

This is documented in the new **Local Setup** section of `CONTRIBUTING.md`, alongside instructions for installing the build toolchain (`xml2rfc` + `kramdown-rfc`).

## Testing

Verified locally: a staged file with trailing spaces and trailing tabs is stripped and re-staged, hook exits 0; a clean file is a no-op.

pulls.title: Rewrite appendix as credential-type-to-property matrix
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
**Merge #36 first.** The second commit here assumes it has landed — see *Merge order* below.

Transposes the appendix so **credential types are rows and properties are columns**, and reconciles it with the body's reorganized property classes.

### The appendix had drifted further than it looked

| Appendix before | Body today |
|---|---|
| §"Presentation Limits" held Validity Window, Selective Disclosure, Audience Restriction | Those moved to **Credential Construction** |
| §"Substantiation" had rows *Integrity* and *Authoritative Relationship* | Renamed **Tamper Proofness** and **Substantiation** |
| §"Credential Containment & Unlock" had a *Dynamism* row | Dynamism moved to **Credential Construction** |
| §"Credential Recovery" had *Recovery Agent / Mechanism / Artifact / Assurance* | **None of these exist in the body anymore**; only Recoverability survives |
| — | **Replayability** and **Referential Identity Posture** were defined in the body but missing from the appendix entirely |

### Rows: 4 → 12 credential types

Added SPIFFE JWT-SVID, mTLS certificate, HOTP, TOTP, SMS OTP, SD-JWT VC, ISO mdoc, and DBSC to the original four.

The additions are what make the property set testable. With only the original four rows, **Selective Disclosure and Chainability were "No" for every row** — columns that differentiated nothing. SD-JWT VC and ISO mdoc exercise both. DBSC is the only row that is contained but *not* activated, and it demonstrates the bounded-replayability point the body makes about OTPs.

### Substantive correction

The old appendix claimed SPIFFE X.509-SVIDs are **"rotated every 5 minutes."** That does not verify — SPIRE's documented default is a **1-hour SVID lifetime rotated at 50% of TTL**. The 5-minute figure appears to be the historical *JWT*-SVID TTL, which changed in SPIRE v0.11.0. I dropped the number rather than restate it.

### Two tables are split

Construction (8 properties) and Containment & Unlock (7) rendered at **116 and 108 columns** — well over the 72-column limit and idnits-failing. Each is now two tables under a single heading, so the 1:1 mapping to the body's classes is preserved. The other four classes are single tables and were already within limits.

### Merge order

The body introduces most of these specifications before the appendix reaches them, so under first-use-only the body owns the citation. Commit 2 here strips those from the appendix, leaving the spec named in plain text, and keeps citations only for what the appendix introduces first (CTAP, SPIFFE, SD-JWT VC, DBSC, PCI DSS, CA/B Forum BR, JWS, Bearer Token Usage).

Merging this **before** #36 would leave those specs uncited. Merging after is clean.

This branch conflicts with #36 in the YAML reference block. **The resolution is a plain union of the two entry lists** — git merges the `normative:`/`informative:` headers cleanly and conflicts only on the entries; no judgment required. I verified the merged result builds, has 0 lines over 72 columns, and that all 26 references are still cited exactly once in the text.

### Verification

- `make` builds clean to `.txt`
- 0 lines exceed the 72-column limit
- All references resolve

Happy to rebase this onto #36 instead if you'd rather Pam not hit the conflict at merge time.

pulls.title: Remove template test draft and ignore .claude/
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
Two cleanups from a pre-publication review of the repository, ahead of making it public and publishing the GitHub Pages site.

Independent of #36 and #37 — this branch touches neither the draft nor the appendix, so it can merge in any order.

### Remove `dingle-test-OLD.md`

Scaffolding left over from the i-d-template bootstrap (a 68-line "Dingle Test Draft"). Nothing references it, and it never matched the `draft-*.md` build glob, so it was never built. It is only clutter for people arriving at a public repo. Verified `make` still builds clean after removal.

### Ignore `.claude/`

The directory was neither tracked nor ignored, so a future `git add -A` could commit local agent configuration. Only `.claude/worktrees/` was excluded, and only via `.git/info/exclude` — which is local to a single checkout and protects nobody who clones the repo.

Added `/.claude/` to the shared `.gitignore`, matching the rooted style already used for `/.idea/`, `/.vscode/` and `/.venv/`.

### Review context

These were the two unambiguous findings from the review. It also checked, and found clean:

- **No credential material in history.** All 122 commits across every branch scanned for cloud access keys, asymmetric key blocks, vendor API keys, signed tokens, and generic assignment patterns — zero hits. No credential or secret-bearing file has ever existed in history.
- **Workflows are safe to publish.** `ghpages.yml` uses `pull_request` rather than `pull_request_target`, so fork PRs get a read-only token and no secrets; the auto-lint-fix step is correctly gated on `head.repo.full_name == github.repository`; only `github.token` is used, no personal access tokens.
- **Issue and PR archive is clean.** 13 issues and 22 PRs, roughly 17K characters of discussion, all technical. No contact addresses or non-public material.
- **No local filesystem paths** leaked into any tracked file.

Three findings were left as judgment calls rather than changes: the author address visible across 49 commits in history, the AI co-authorship line in `research-report.md`, and GitHub Actions pinned to mutable major tags rather than commit SHAs.

pulls.title: Add a chained referential identity example and anchor the postures
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
Carries forward one commit that missed the squash merge of #36. Rebuilt on current `main`.

Referential Identity Posture defines seven postures but illustrated only three — Delegated, Impersonated and Partitioned. **Chained had no example at all.**

### Chained

Cites transaction tokens (`draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens`, OAuth WG, rev 11, WG consensus reached). They preserve the identity of the original caller as a request traverses a call chain of workloads, and §13.15 requires that when a transaction token is replaced, the service **MUST** maintain the chain of workloads that requested the prior token in the newly issued one.

That is the transitive relationship the posture describes, expressed as a normative requirement rather than an incidental property — which is what makes it a stronger example than a system that merely happens to produce a chain.

The text also notes that token exchange encodes the same structure directly through nested `act` claims, where the outermost actor is the current party and each nested actor a prior one.

### Delegated and Impersonated

Both postures were defined descriptively. RFC 8693 §1.1 already draws the distinction normatively: a delegated actor retains its own identity while acting as an agent for another party, whereas an impersonating actor gains that party's rights and is indistinguishable from it. The definitions are now anchored to that wording.

RFC 8693 is already cited two sentences earlier in the same section, so it is not cited again — consistent with the first-use-only convention established in #36.

### Verification

- `make` builds clean
- 0 lines exceed the 72-column limit
- 18 references, each cited exactly once and listed once

### Note

`draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens` is an active draft targeting IESG submission in December 2026. If it publishes as an RFC before this document does, the citation will need updating — as will `draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc`, referenced in the appendix work.

pulls.title: Build the rich PDF via xml2rfc, with weasyprint opt-in
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
Commits the rich PDF build, which until now existed only in one working tree and so worked on exactly one machine.

The template's default rule (`lib/main.mk:148`) pipes the plain text output through `enscript | ps2pdf`, producing a typewriter-style PDF with no hyperlinks, no bookmarks and no real fonts. This overrides it with `xml2rfc --pdf`, producing the datatracker-style document.

### What CI taught us — the important part

The first attempt committed the dependency as `requirements.txt`. **That broke the build outright**, and the failure is worth recording because it is a trap for contributors too:

```
"pip3" install -q --no-user -r requirements.txt          ← succeeded
...
File "/usr/lib/python3.14/site-packages/xml2rfc/__init__.py", line 38
    from weasyprint.text.ffi import pango
KeyError: 'weasyprint'
make[1]: *** [lib/main.mk:98: draft-...xml] Error 1
make: *** [lib/main.mk:20: all] Error 2
```

Two mechanisms combine:

1. `lib/deps.mk:143` globs the **exact literal** `requirements.txt` and installs it automatically, including in CI.
2. `xml2rfc` imports weasyprint's FFI layer **at module load** whenever weasyprint is present.

The container has no pango, so that import raised and `xml2rfc` would not start at all. This took down the `xml`, `txt` and `html` builds — the PDF target was never even reached, since no workflow invokes it.

So installing weasyprint where pango is absent does not degrade the PDF build; it destroys the whole toolchain.

### The fix

Name the file **`requirements-pdf.txt`**. `deps.mk` does not glob it, so nothing is installed automatically and CI is untouched. Anyone who wants the rich PDF opts in:

```
pip install -r requirements-pdf.txt
# macOS:          brew install pango
# Debian/Ubuntu:  apt-get install libpango-1.0-0 libpangoft2-1.0-0
```

The file documents this in its own header, so the next person to find it learns why the name matters before they rename it back.

`.gitignore` gains a matching `!requirements-pdf.txt` negation, since `*.txt` on line 5 would otherwise swallow it — the same reason the template already carries `!requirements.txt`.

The `Makefile` rule is safe to commit unconditionally: it is a static pattern rule whose explicit targets take precedence over the generic `%.pdf: %.txt` pattern, and it is inert until weasyprint is installed. No workflow calls `make pdf`.

### Verified

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `make all` — exactly what CI runs | clean (kramdown-rfc, xml2rfc-txt, xml2rfc-html all OK) |
| `make pdf` — with weasyprint installed | 85KB datatracker-style PDF |
| `deps.mk` auto-install | no longer triggered — glob is for the literal `requirements.txt` |

### Follow-up worth considering

Nothing in CI exercises `make pdf`, so the PDF path stays unverified on Linux. If that matters, a `pdf` step could be added to `ghpages.yml` — but it would need pango and cairo in the i-d-template container, which is exactly what this PR just demonstrated is missing. Probably better left as a documented local-only build.

pulls.title: Add ID-JAG to the credential-type appendix
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
Closes #46.

Adds the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG, draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant) as a credential type in the appendix "Applying the Properties to Common Credential Types": a description bullet and one row in each of the nine property tables, placed after the sender-constrained access token.

Property values follow the -06 text (31 October 2026):

- A bearer assertion by default, with optional DPoP or mTLS binding via a `cnf` claim (§9.11). The resource authorization server SHOULD require client authentication and MUST reject a request with neither client authentication nor a sender-constrained ID-JAG (§4.4), so Replayability is "Replayable unless bound by `cnf`" and Containment is "Uncontained; Proactive when sender-constrained".
- Clients MAY re-submit the same ID-JAG after the access token expires, and single use by `jti` is something the resource authorization server "can" do rather than a requirement (§4.4.4), so Validity Count is "Unlimited within the validity window".
- Short lifetimes are recommended and clients SHOULD NOT cache the grant (§9.2).
- Referential Identity Posture is Delegated (`sub` plus `client_id`), Chained when the optional `act` claim is present.

Adds informative references to the draft and to RFC 7523. RFC 8693 is not re-cited in the bullet because token exchange is already cited in the Referential Identity Posture section.

`make all` passes: no trailing whitespace, both new references resolve, rendered reference shows revision -06.

pulls.title: Add Unlinkability property and BBS credential row for ZKP credentials
pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
Closes #48.

Raised by Nick Steele (OpenAI): the property set had no way to describe a zero-knowledge-proof credential. SD-JWT and "a ZKP" were offered as interchangeable examples of Selective Disclosure, and a BBS credential scored the same as an SD-JWT VC in the appendix.

## Changes

- **New property: Unlinkability** (Credential Presentation, after Replayability, anchor `{#unlinkability}`). Valued: Linkable / Verifier-unlinkable / Issuer-unlinkable, following the taxonomy in RFC 9901 Section 10.1. Per-verifier pseudonymity is described as a mode of an issuer-unlinkable credential, citing `draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-per-verifier-linkability`. The text states that unlinkability is independent of Referential Identity Posture.
- **Selective Disclosure is now valued**: None / Per-claim / Predicate. SD-JWT and ZKP are no longer presented as equivalents. A closing sentence cross-references Unlinkability so that the W3C framing of unlinkable disclosure as a kind of selective disclosure is addressed explicitly rather than by accident.
- **Posture examples** added for Pseudonymous (per-verifier pseudonym) and Anonymous (Privacy Pass token; BBS proof over non-identifying claims), which previously had none.
- **Appendix A**: a BBS verifiable credential row in every table, an Unlinkability column in the Presentation table filled for all rows, and the Selective Disclosure column moved from Yes/No to the new values.
- **References added**: `I-D.irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures` (-14), `I-D.irtf-cfrg-bbs-per-verifier-linkability` (-03), RFC 9577 (Privacy Pass), and W3C `vc-di-bbs` as a Candidate Recommendation Draft dated 2026-09-10.

## Decisions taken (per discussion on #48)

1. One valued property rather than separate verifier- and issuer-unlinkability properties.
2. RFC 9901's taxonomy as the value set, not the W3C identifier/signature/metadata correlation split, which is described in prose as the correlation vectors.
3. Predicate Proof folded into Selective Disclosure as a value instead of a new property. No current appendix row scores Predicate; the BBS row notes that predicates need a range proof beyond the base scheme.
4. `vc-di-bbs` is cited. It is a CR Draft from September 2026, not the 2024 Working Draft the issue assumed.
5. No Privacy Pass appendix row; it appears as a prose example only. No ETSI TR 119 476 citation; RFC 9901 carries the point.

## Review notes

- The BBS Containment cell states that the holder secret is protected only by wallet software because proof generation consumes the secret and hardware secure elements do not typically offer BBS operations. This is stronger than the other rows say and is worth a second look.
- `make all` passes. The two rendered lines over 72 columns are pre-existing bullets with multi-byte dashes.
- Conflicts with #43 (class intro line) and #47 (Presentation table: #47 adds the ID-JAG row, this adds a column). Suggested order: merge #43, #44 and #47 first, then this branch is rebased and the ID-JAG Unlinkability cell filled as Linkable.
